title: Ghosts in Florida city hall? Group wants to provide tours
excerpt: Larry Lawson, owner of Indian River Hauntings, wants to give tours of Fellsmere City Hall, where, he says, paranormal investigators have experienced activity.
content:
Oct. 5, 2026, 5:03 a.m. ET

Not everyone would consider a visit to City Hall fun or interesting.

Larry Lawson, owner of Indian River Hauntings, thinks otherwise. He's hoping to resume his Fellsmere ghost tours, taking groups through Fellsmere City Hall after dark — on nights when the City Council isn't meeting, of course.

Fellsmere City Hall, located in the former Fellsmere School, 21 S. Cypress St., is filled with interesting stories of unexplained phenomena, Lawson explained.

"People started telling me about the crazy things happening out there," said Lawson, who's been interested in the paranormal for many years. A former law enforcement officer and the retired director of the Indian River State College police academy, previously worked part-time as a Fellsmere Police Department detective.

Lawson and his team of paranormal investigators, called the Florida Bureau of Paranormal Investigation, started doing some research.

"There was activity out there we couldn't explain," he said.

The City Council was ready on Oct. 1 to consider a contract with Lawson and Indian River Hauntings that would allow the tours, but the item was moved to the Oct. 15 meeting, city officials said.

Lawson said it's been about five years since he last led a tour in Fellsmere, which included visits to Marsh Landing Restaurant, the Fellsmere Inn and the Marian Fell Library. He wants to resume, but the city wanted to have a contract, and it must be approved before he can resume any tours, he said.

Among phenomena the team has experienced at the school is the spirit of a young boy, who indicated his name could be Billy.

The team has made contact with Billy on a few occasions, he said. Once, the team was in the Fellsmere City Hall auditorium when one member used the team's specialized equipment to ask, "Billy, is this the room you like to be in?"

"Clear as a bell — and you can hear it better with earphones, but you can certainly hear it without," Lawson said, "you hear a little boy respond, saying, 'Yes, Sir.'"

On one tour, the group experienced a door handle wiggle, but there was no one there, he said. Those working in the building have told him about children talking with other unseen children, and other unexplained happenings, he said.

He's hoping to hold the tours once a month, maybe more if there is interest. Private tours also could be arranged, he said. Guided tours would occur year-round, he said.

The tours are about more than just ghost stories, he said.

"It's about sharing the history and helping people realize what Fellsmere is, what the history is out there, what Fellsmere has to offer (and) what Fellsmere has done to help shape the country," Lawson said. "So it covers a multitude of different aspects.

"It's more of an experience where my team would get out there and we would show people how we use our equipment," he said. "We allow them to use it. And a lot of times, they were able to experience things that we couldn't explain. "

Lawson warned that while the tour contains no "jump scares" nor is it intended to frighten people, children might get bored with hearing stories about history.

Tours would cost $20 for anyone older than 11, with discount tickets for children 5-11. The city would receive 25% of the proceeds from the tours, according to the contract.

Colleen Wixon is the Indian River County government watchdog reporter for TCPalm and Treasure Coast Newspapers.
